title: Justice
hookLine: do justly (Micah 6:8) in one place you can
tomorrow: Nia asks Grace, "be honest: was my speech bad?" what does she say?

lines: CHANGE THE TIRE, OR FIX THE HOLE?
cards: A pothole on one street keeps wrecking tires. You could help each driver change a flat, or you could get the city to fix the hole. Christians argue, warmly, over which of those justice mostly is.

Both sides quote the same line from the prophet Micah: “He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?”
Today, both sides get to speak.

teach.b: One view starts with hands. In Jesus' story of the Samaritan, nobody repairs the Jericho road. One man stops, binds up a stranger's wounds, and pays the innkeeper.
On this view, justice is mostly mercy up close: the meal, the covered shift, the person right in front of you. Rules change; a neighbor who stops is what lasts. The other view starts with the road.

teach.h: THE ROAD: LET JUDGMENT RUN DOWN.
teach.b: Amos cries: “let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.” Isaiah says: “seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.”
That's courts, wages, rules that crush people quietly. On this view, helping one person at a time while the hole stays open isn't enough.

teach.h: OPEN THY MOUTH FOR THE POOR.
teach.b: Proverbs adds: “Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy.” Each side has a best case, and each can see something the other might miss.
Micah keeps them in one sentence: do justly, and love mercy, side by side.
And today's practice is small enough for either side: one fairness, in one place you can reach.

how: Christians work for justice in different ways: food banks and shelters, legal aid, prison ministry, and speaking up for fair laws and wages; churches differ on how much to stress each.

o: punishment that matches the wrongdoer's crime
making things right for people, hands and rules
keeping out of other people's business

games.q: two sides of justice — tap the pairs.
p: let judgment run down as waters
plead the cause of the poor

s: Micah asks for mercy instead of justice
do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly: all three in one line.
Christians all agree whether justice means charity or changing rules
some start with hands, like the Samaritan; others with the road, like Amos.
Amos pictures justice like a river
let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.

games.q: you run the school food drive. your friend says food drives are band-aids and only changing the rules counts. what is her best case, in her own terms?
o: Amos: let judgment run down as waters. if the rules keep making hunger, fix those too.
she just doesn't want to do the work of running a food drive.
the Samaritan story proves that helping one person is pointless.
games.why: her steelman is Amos and Isaiah: justice for the whole road. yours is the Samaritan who stopped. Micah keeps both in one sentence.

practice: Think of one unfairness you can actually reach: a chore that always lands on the same person, a classmate always left out, a schedule that keeps hitting one coworker.
Name the fair outcome you want, name what will stop you, and decide your first move: when that happens, I'll do this. If you pray, ask for courage for that one move.

wordCard.voice: Justice. Making things right for people, by the hand that helps and the voice that changes the rule.

orig.note: Hebrew: justice, judgment, what's right. 'to do justly' in Micah 6:8 is to do mishpat.

carryVoice: The line to keep: do justly, right beside the mercy, in one place you can reach. That's day 1732.
